item.title: Argos: A Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture for Distributed Edge Security Orchestration
item.description: arXiv:2610.14019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing adoption of distributed edge devices for security auditing and operational monitoring exposes limitations in lightweight control mechanisms traditionally used to manage such nodes. While commercial Command-and-Control (C2) platforms offer advanced orchestration features, their licensing constraints, operational complexity, and proprietary nature limit accessibility for small and medium-sized enterprises and research environments. This paper presents Argos, a multi-tenant SaaS C2 architecture designed for transparent, automated, and long-term orchestration of distributed edge devices. The framework implements a structured control plane with role-based access control (RBAC), tenant isolation, persistent task management, and cron-based workflow automation. Unlike operator-driven or stateless execution models, Argos enables scheduled and autonomous coordination of security tasks across heterogeneous environments. To formally substantiate its isolation guarantees, the platform is modeled through a set-theoretic authorization framework, and a tenant non-interference property is proven. The proposed architecture was evaluated across three geographically distributed edge devices, executing 810 automated tasks mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Results demonstrate a global failure rate of 3.33% (95% Wilson confidence interval: [2.30%, 4.81%]) with no statistically significant difference across ARM and x86 architectures (\c{hi} 2 = 1.55, p = 0.21), and stable operation under heterogeneous latency conditions, including intercontinental deployments. To ensure scientific transparency and reproducibility, the evaluation methodology, sanitized datasets, and statistical scripts have been made publicly available in an open-source repository.
item.dc:creator: Agustin Javier Di Bartolo, Mohammadhossein Homaei, Andres Caro, Mar Avila

item.title: Symmetric Cryptography via Dirichlet Convolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.14040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss a new symmetric-key cipher for digital data encryption. Its implementation is fast, memory efficient, and resilient against classical, AI-assisted, and quantum attacks. Let $x$, $k$, and $c$ be elements of a finite abelian group $G$ with operation $+$ and neutral element $0$. Suppose one is given ciphertext $c=x+k$. Retrieving the plaintext $x=c-k$ from the ciphertext is trivial when the key $k$ is known. Without the key, however, recovering $x$ amounts to a blind search. Even if an efficient criterion were available for identifying the plaintext among all group elements, the average number of trials would remain prohibitively large when the group is sufficiently large. The challenge in constructing a practical cryptosystem is therefore to identify a sufficiently rich group $G$, together with efficient algorithms that enable an immersion of \emph{real digital data} into $G$ and efficient evaluation of the group operations. The proposed cipher is based on generalized Dirichlet convolution over finite fields. We investigate its security against plaintext attacks from an information-theoretic perspective. The nonlocal structure of Dirichlet convolution naturally permits plaintext salting, providing protection against plaintext attacks while allowing controlled key reuse. We establish perfect masking properties over finite fields and prove that the resulting cipher achieves information-theoretic security under key reuse when the underlying arithmetic is carried out in $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>2$. For arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_2$, some information leakage remains, leading to a finite key-reuse budget.
item.dc:creator: Artur Sowa, Elias Hassani Sangani, Francis Bui, Grant Harris, Jonathan Norton

item.title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.14089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
item.dc:creator: Zhimin Li, Pan Wang, Jingxian Chen, Yuantao Tang, Qian Lou, Jingtong Hu

item.title: An Empirical Case Study of Prompt Engineering Strategies for Bypassing Multi-Layer Agent Security Defenses
item.description: arXiv:2610.14116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The OpenClaw Security Attack and Defense Challenge evaluates AI agent robustness through a three-stage defense pipeline: skill file scanning (Stage 1), instruction safety evaluation (Stage 2), and attack trajectory scoring (Stage 3). This paper presents an empirical case study of prompt engineering strategies against these layers across 19 attack targets in Enterprise OA, E-commerce, and Smart Home scenarios. I document both successful and failed strategies, with an emphasis on the observed trade-off between instruction safety (Stage 2) and attack execution accuracy (Stage 3). The final online score is 0.2630, with 5 of 19 tasks achieving full bypass. The results suggest that multi-layer defenses, reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints, substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.
item.dc:creator: Chengwei Chu

item.title: TrustPaper for forged PDF with Issuer Fingerprints
item.description: arXiv:2610.14132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sick leave certificates are increasingly delivered as PDF files by online teleconsultation platforms, and can be altered in minutes with free editors. Generic PDF scanners report how a file was built, but cannot tell whether that construction is legitimate: an incremental update, an embedded font or a given producer string is normal for one issuer and anomalous for another. We present TrustPaper solution, an issuer aware forensic approach that combines three elements: the claimed issuer of the document, a reference fingerprint learned beforehand from genuine documents of that issuer, and an explainable combination of evidence from several forensic modules. Fingerprints are stored as versioned declarative profiles, and every anomaly keeps its observed value, expected value and triggering rule. We formalize the threat model, the fingerprint and the scoring model, and evaluate the open-source prototype on a controlled corpus documents from two issuers and six forgery techniques. With the issuer fingerprint, all forgeries made by opportunistic and metadata-aware attackers are flagged with no false positive on genuine test documents.
item.dc:creator: Yassine El Jakani, Mohamed Nadir Rhazi, Othmane Meknassi, Oualid Chbiki, Mounira Msahli, Francois Gonnet

item.title: Memory-Coupled Unlearning for Data-Absent Identity Forgetting
item.description: arXiv:2610.14148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to reduce the influence of designated training data from a trained model while preserving its utility on retained data. Identity-level unlearning is particularly challenging when only limited target-specific information is available when a forgetting request is processed. In this work, we propose Memory-Coupled Unlearning (MCU), a framework that augments a host model with a Modern Hopfield Network (MHN) serving as a controllable external identity-prototype memory. During prototype construction, feature representations associated with each training identity are aggregated into identity prototypes and stored in the MHN. A Prototype Adaptation Network (PAN) transforms the retrieved memory representation, while a Dependency Gating Unit (DGU) controls its contribution to downstream prediction. When an identity is requested to be forgotten, MCU first removes the corresponding prototype from the external memory and subsequently readapts the model using limited support information associated with the target identities together with retained data. Importantly, in this work, ``data-absent'' specifically refers to the absence of the complete original forget set during request-time gradient-based readaptation; retained data may still be used to preserve downstream-task utility. Experiments based on the identity-partitioning and one-shot support construction of 1-SHUI show that MCU achieves a favorable empirical trade-off among model utility, membership distinguishability, and request-time computational efficiency compared with the evaluated baselines. These results provide empirical evidence for the potential of controllable external memory in machine unlearning, rather than a formal guarantee of complete information removal.
item.dc:creator: Chun-I Fan, Lu-En Chen, Ming-Feng Tsai, Tomohiro Morikawa

item.title: Embedding Asymmetry as Attack Signal: Detecting and Defending Active Label Inference in Vertical Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vertical federated learning lets organizations train a shared model over features they hold separately, while one party keeps the labels private. The active label inference attack of Fu et al. [12] breaks this: a feature-holding party runs a modified optimizer, MaliciousSGD, that forces class structure into its embeddings and then recovers the labels with semi-supervised learning. Defenses that perturb the shared gradient fail, because the attack acts on the party's internal optimizer, not on the message it sends. We show the attack leaves a signal the server can read from the embeddings it already receives. The adversary's Fisher class-separability pulls away from the honest party's, and the gap is visible within a few epochs. A defense triggered by this signal acts on the adversary alone. Scaling its gradient down handles few-class tasks, and a norm non-expansive projection handles many-class tasks, with the Discriminative Coverage Ratio explaining why the projection rank must grow with the class count. The defense breaks the alignment between embedding clusters and labels rather than destroying the embedding. Across four seeds on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10, label inference falls below what honest training already leaks, at under two points of task-accuracy cost.
item.dc:creator: Soumya Swagata Biswas, Muhammad Abdullah Adnan

item.title: Physical Side-Channel Attacks on Edge LLMs: Extracting Output Tokens and User Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2610.14215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices is largely motivated by privacy concerns over sharing sensitive user data with cloud servers. In this paper, we demonstrate that keeping inference local does not eliminate privacy risks: an adversary with physical access to the device may exploit hardware leakage to recover sensitive information without compromising or modifying the software system. In particular, we present an electromagnetic (EM) side-channel attack targeting LLM inference on edge devices. Targeting LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct running on a Raspberry Pi 5, we demonstrate that EM traces collected during inference can leak both generated tokens and user prompts. We propose three attacks under different threat assumptions. First, a profiling attack that identifies generated tokens among 50 medical and privacy-related keywords with 97.2% accuracy on profiled words. Second, a reconstruction attack recovers the model's hidden representations and uses them to predict tokens from the full 128k-token vocabulary, achieving 94.3% accuracy on profiled classes. For unseen words, the correct token is ranked within the first 100 positions of the 128k-token vocabulary in 67% of cases, with a median rank of 54. Finally, we present a hidden-state inversion attack that uses the recovered hidden state to reconstruct user prompts semantically. Our proposed attacks require only passive EM side-channel measurements and a limited number of traces during model training. These results demonstrate that local execution alone may not guarantee the confidentiality of generated tokens and user inputs.
item.dc:creator: Najeh Alhalawani, Gunes Acar, Zhuoran Liu, Lejla Batina

item.title: Watermarking for Byzantine Robust LLM Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.14289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM watermarking has emerged as a promising approach for detecting downstream model misuse in centralized settings, but extending it to federated learning (FL) presents unique challenges. In particular, FL systems often rely on strong robust aggregators to defend against poisoning attacks. We empirically show that a malicious server can exploit these same aggregators as effective watermark-removal mechanisms during training, causing representative existing LLM watermarking methods to fail detection in the final model. To address this limitation, we formalize the problem as a constrained optimization task and propose CamoMark, an aggregator-agnostic watermarking scheme for embedding robust watermarks in FL. CamoMark optimizes watermarked updates to become inliers, maintaining bounded deviation from the distribution of clean updates, while preserving sufficient watermark signal for reliable detection. Evaluated on Qwen fine-tuned on the Alpaca dataset, CamoMark achieves a detection confidence of $p$-value $= 1.82\times10^{-2}$ using only 3.3% watermarked data. The watermark also remains robust to a range of post-training removal attacks, including continued fine-tuning on clean data, pruning, and model distillation. At higher watermark ratios, detection confidence improves substantially, reaching $p$-value $= 5.11\times10^{-11}$ at a 13.3% watermark ratio.
item.dc:creator: Leixu Huang, Zedian Shao, Teodora Baluta

item.title: ARMOR: Adversary Cost Amplification via a Schema-Preserving Password-Hardening Retrofit for Resource-Constrained Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.14300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) gateways, edge authentication servers, and legacy systems need protection against offline password guessing after credential-database disclosure. Memory-hard key derivation functions (KDFs) are the preferred defense, but their resource requirements can exceed memory or latency budgets. ARMOR addresses this gap with a schema-preserving verifier-side transform for database-only (DB-only) compromise. Secret per-account chains of injective operations reside in an isolated Chain Registry. Fixed terminal escape encoding preserves distinct pre-hash values under each chain and moves outputs outside printable ASCII. We evaluate NAIVE adversaries using unmodified cracking tools and AWARE adversaries that enumerate chains. For the evaluated pre-hardened three-operation chains, NAIVE recovery is at most 0.10% on non-digit targets. Escape encoding yields zero recovery of digit-only targets under evaluated stock rule-based and non-rule attacks, closing a bypass permitting up to 45.3% recovery. Across 14.05 million eligible RockYou password entries, retaining duplicates, the median conditional guessing number is approximately 52 output-class tests at depth three and 317 at depth five. These values quantify the chain-search subproblem given the correct plaintext under a unit-cost model. A separate historical 14-operation AWARE evaluation matches all transformed targets at full dictionary coverage. Deployment measurements show microsecond-scale bare-metal transforms on three IoT boards, with protected storage dominating the measured TrustZone-M prototype components. Although an isolated high-entropy pepper provides stronger cryptographic protection, ARMOR combines compact per-account chain storage with low transform cost. When resources permit and the KDF accepts the complete transformed output, ARMOR composes as KDF(ARMOR(password)).
item.dc:creator: Avinash Srinivasan

item.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.14350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.
item.dc:creator: Jie Zhu, Ronik Bhaskar, Heather Zheng, Ben Y. Zhao, Kexin Pei

item.title: Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking: A Byte-Local Method for LLM Text
item.description: arXiv:2610.14378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (TI-WM), a method that embeds a watermark during token generation but keys and scores it on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes. The detector does not invoke the tokenizer. Canonicalizer-preserving edits leave its score unchanged; other localized canonical-byte edits affect a bounded number of scoring windows. Across three fixed keys and 128 prompts per key and model, a deterministic white-box attack at a 5% word-edit budget leaves mean attacked-AUC 0.530 on Qwen3-8B and 0.664 on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with 0.410 and 0.489 for Unigram with detection-side deletion. These operating points are not jointly matched on quality and clean detectability. Bias sweeps show model-dependent distortion costs, and shared-rule controls support a locality interpretation without establishing a unique advantage of bytes. Visible insertion outside the canonicalizer's deletion set defeats the default design. Alphabetic filtering closes that channel but does not resolve source shift or calibrated detection power. TI-WM thus provides a concrete construction with local scoring guarantees and measured attack-ranking gains, not a general robustness or low-false-positive-rate deployment guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Tung-Ling Li

item.title: DICE: Tilting the Odds through Interface Attackson System One Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.14404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One models offer typed judgments that applications can turn into decisions. Their answers, however, are conditional on the state and question supplied by surrounding components, and on how the application uses the response. We study this boundary in a Jev-based pipeline with bounded substitutions at three adapter outputs: state extraction, question generation, and output interpretation. Across three small synthetic studies, each adapter can change the final decision while Jev and its authentic API responses remain outside attacker control. The cases expose distinct failures of source fidelity, answer meaning, and response relevance. Checks that bind these relationships stopped the corresponding interventions we tested, although source verification also rejected some valid clean decisions. The pilot identifies where correct request-level judgments can lose their connection to the original task; it does not estimate the prevalence of these failures in deployed systems.
item.dc:creator: Ben Dong, Tianyi Lu, Zhonghao Guo, Qian Wang

item.title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.
item.dc:creator: Xiaopu Wang, Runze Li

item.title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.
item.dc:creator: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang

item.title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.
item.dc:creator: Ruidong Han, Zhensu Sun, Chengyan Ma, Yuqing Niu, Siqi Ma, David Lo

item.title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Commey

item.title: Decision Uncertainty-Oriented Watermarking (DUOW): Securing Multi-Agent Routing Against Policy Cloning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routing policies in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) represent valuable intellectual property, yet their exposure through execution logs creates significant risks of unauthorized policy cloning. Existing agent watermarking methods protect intellectual property by modifying internal generation processes, such as perturbing token sampling distributions or injecting structural mutations into action trajectories, which may compromise task fidelity or suffer from limited transferability across heterogeneous platforms. To address these limitations, we propose Decision Uncertainty-Oriented Watermarking (DUOW), a lightweight framework that operates at the external decision layer without modifying model parameters or generated outputs. DUOW introduces a plug-and-play scoring mechanism that evaluates candidate agents from semantic and operational perspectives, identifies functionally redundant routing decisions, and selectively redirects choices among equivalent alternatives to embed ownership signals. By coupling watermark behaviors with utility-preserving routing decisions, DUOW enables cloned policies to retain ownership signals during policy imitation while increasing the difficulty of watermark removal. A confidence-driven adaptive threshold dynamically determines embedding opportunities, balancing watermark capacity and task fidelity under diverse routing contexts. Extensive evaluations on four multi-agent routing benchmarks demonstrate that DUOW preserves high task utility, achieves reliable ownership verification under up to 90% log erasure, and introduces negligible computational overhead, with an average per-step latency of 0.043 ms and total embedding overhead below 0.54 ms.
item.dc:creator: Ziming Zhang, Li Li, Guorui Feng, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang, Athanasios V. Vasilakos

item.title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). OMCB remains dormant and undetectable within one standalone model but activates upon merging, triggering safety unalignment. We first theoretically analyze the existence and geometric location of OMCB, revealing that the parameter shift crossing safety decision boundaries is the main cause of backdoor activation. Building upon this insight, we propose SMOKE, a meta-learning-based attack framework. SMOKE implants OMCB via a bi-level optimization strategy: the inner loop synthesizes surrogate meta-vectors through random low-rank initialization and finite-step maximization, while the outer loop optimizes the target model by simulating the merging process. Furthermore, preliminary analysis shows that the injected OMCB has bounded generalization loss under unknown merging configurations. Extensive experiments across diverse model architectures and merging techniques validate the effectiveness of SMOKE and its resistance to existing backdoor detections, highlighting a significant yet previously overlooked vulnerability in the model merging paradigm.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Chen, Yidou Chen, Yiming Li, Xinyu Zhang, Baosong Yang, Hongwei Yao, Zhan Qin

item.title: No, Your Tools Are Not Enough: It's Time to Bring Agents to the Hunt
item.description: arXiv:2610.14729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern software systems are large and complex, demanding scalable and autonomous techniques for vulnerability discovery. Existing approaches still depend on human expertise for domain knowledge, and on human intervention throughout the process of vulnerability discovery. AI agents offer us an opportunity to make vulnerability discovery more adaptive, scalable, and autonomous. Agents bring the ability to make continuous decisions and adapt, and general knowledge that can be augmented. In this paper, we present our experience using AI agents to find vulnerabilities across diverse programs such as Windows drivers, the Linux kernel, XNU, firmware, and web applications. We use an iterative agentic workflow and find that it generalizes across these targets. We discuss tasks that agents help with, which were previously challenging, and some future research directions we consider important for advancing autonomous vulnerability discovery.
item.dc:creator: Ati Priya Bajaj, Xiang Mei, Tiffany Bao, Yan Shoshitaishvili, Ruoyu Wang, Adam Doup\'e

item.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?
item.description: arXiv:2610.14766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Wu, Chao Ge, Peng Chen, Fengji Zhang, Yongxing Wu, Yuchong Xie, Jian Li, Chaoyuan Peng, Kaikai Zhang, Dong Huang, Mingzhe Du, Yukai Huang, Jiaheng Zhang, Terry Yue Zhuo, See-Kiong Ng

item.title: When Does Trust Help? A Leakage-Free Evaluation of Representation- and Aggregation-Based Defenses Against Backdoors in Federated Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.14767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets distributed intrusion-detection systems (IDS) train on private traffic, but exposes the global model to poisoning and backdoor attacks under non-IID client data. A popular defense family scores or filters clients using a small trusted "root" dataset and the similarity of client behaviour to a trusted reference. I re-examine these trust-based defenses under a protocol designed to remove common evaluation artifacts: train-only feature standardization, a server root set disjoint from client data, multi-seed (n=6) runs with paired significance tests, formal (varepsilon, delta) accounting for DP-SGD, and a defense-aware adaptive attacker. Across three NIDS datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, NF-ToN-IoT, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) I find: (1) a representation-similarity aggregator (RepGuard) significantly improves classification utility and seed-stability over FLTrust under heavy non-IID poisoning, and - under severe heterogeneity or many adversaries - also lowers backdoor ASR substantially (e.g., 0.48 vs FLTrust 0.86 at Dirichlet alpha=0.1); (2) at strong trigger magnitudes no defense reduces backdoor attack success rate (ASR approx 0.95); (3) a controlled trigger-magnitude sweep shows defenses help only for small triggers (ASR 0.10 for RepGuard at magnitude 0.5, vs. 0.40 undefended) and collapse to ASR approx 1.0 by magnitude 2; (4) a triggered-canary check that assumes knowledge of the attacker's trigger - the assumption behind much prior "success" - lowers ASR from 0.49 to 0.12, i.e., trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses the backdoor; (5) correctly-accounted DP-SGD (varepsilon in [0.3, 16]) costs little utility but does not mitigate the backdoor. I release the protocol so future FL-IDS defenses can be evaluated without the leakage and oracle assumptions that inflate reported robustness.
item.dc:creator: Shiddarth Dey Tusar, Zawad Yalmie Sazid

item.title: Protecting Shared Agent Workflows from Invalidation Attacks with Signed Trajectories and Runtime Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.14795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on shared workflow repositories to transfer experience across tasks and agents. By abstracting past executions into reusable workflow graphs, such systems significantly improve planning efficiency and generalization. However, this emerging paradigm introduces a new and underexplored security risk: if the shared repository is compromised, tampered workflows can systematically mislead downstream agents, inducing persistent execution failures or unsafe behaviors. In this work, we present a principled protection framework for shared agent workflows based on signed trajectories and runtime verification. We require all cloud-collected trajectories used for workflow generation to be cryptographically signed, with each trajectory representing a concrete execution instance. Prior to repository inclusion, trajectories undergo a unified screening process to ensure correctness and validity. When an agent retrieves a workflow from the shared repository, it also obtains a small set of signed supporting trajectories and verifies both their cryptographic integrity and their semantic consistency with the workflow. To make this practical for branching workflows, we further propose a runtime, path-aware retrieval strategy that dynamically fetches only the signed trajectories relevant to the execution path actually taken by the agent, substantially reducing communication and verification overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates, degrading agent inference performance by up to 73.16 percentage points in accuracy without effective workflow protection. In addition, the proposed protection achieves an average F1 score of 85.26% and a detection rate of 79.97%, outperforming existing baselines by about 2.02x.
item.dc:creator: Ruixiao Li, Fahao Chen, Peng Li

item.title: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a key extension mechanism for agent systems, Agent Skills package specialized capabilities for reuse by LLM agents. An agent first retrieves candidate skills based on skill documentation and then relies on their metadata to make the final selection. As third-party skills proliferate on insufficiently vetted open registry platforms, the security risks posed by malicious skills become increasingly prominent, but existing attack research still focuses primarily on the potential harm caused after their execution. The limited related studies typically examine skill retrieval or selection in isolation and have yet to cover a complete end-to-end attack chain. To address this research gap, we find an end-to-end attack surface arising from the process-wide influence of metadata. Based on this finding, we propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end metadata-only poisoning framework. MetaCascade first generates diverse malicious skill candidates through multi-view semantic expansion, then uses tasks and black-box competition feedback to analyze the competitive relationships among malicious candidate skills and iteratively optimize malicious metadata, thereby improving the target skill's end-to-end attack effectiveness. Under a unified evaluation setting spanning four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, MetaCascade achieves state-of-the-art attack performance, with its average attack success rate (ASR) and its average ASR under four defense settings exceeding the strongest baselines under the corresponding settings by 35.53 and 34.65 percentage points, respectively. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.
item.dc:creator: Junhao Wen, Ping Deng, Qizhi Chen, Junchen Li, Shuang Liang

item.title: StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine
item.description: arXiv:2610.14849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authenticated state transitions need proof engines that conserve memory, avoid repeated setup, and preserve request semantics across parallel execution. We present StateSync-GKR, a reusable Rust sumcheck/GKR core with a sparse-Merkle frontend, and connect its design mechanisms to controlled measurements. Sparse layer reduction and derived wiring reduce prover ownership and repeated verification work. Cube/affine fusion and parallel path constraints keep the circuit schedule and proof-size growth compact. Reusable preparation and indexed parallel jobs amortize setup while maintaining independent results. Three-state records, strict original-request decoding, and separate core/model interfaces expose the application and assurance boundaries. With circuit, field, transcript and prover driver held fixed, sparse reduction lowers additional requested allocation 3,242-fold and peak process resident memory 89.46-fold relative to StateSync-GKR's test-only dense reference for a two-layer mixed circuit of width 4096. Direct depth-24 fresh/prepared measurements show 3.46-4.45-fold lower per-request proving-path latency. CPU and full-proof delivery studies distinguish useful parallel work from queueing and return-path costs, retaining all outcomes and latency budgets. The evaluation supports larger circuits within finite RAM, lower repeated-request cost, and explicit deployment choices for this artifact. It preserves the cryptographic claim boundary of the existing construction.
item.dc:creator: Jinwook Kim

item.title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.
item.dc:creator: Varun Gadey, Markus Tohn, Lichao Wu, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, Alexandra Dmitrienko

item.title: When the Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity for Deployment and Coding-Agent Approvals
item.description: arXiv:2610.15137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment tool's own record of its inputs or a manifest declared in the repository.
item.dc:creator: Md Imran Hossen

item.title: The Agent Clicks Approve: Injected Page Text Makes Browser Agents Authorize Access the Task Never Named
item.description: arXiv:2610.15138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A browser agent that works in its user's signed-in session can be steered by a two-sentence note on a page it reads into approving a third party's access to the user's account. The agent is a confused deputy: the session supplies the authority, the page designates the access request to approve or the webhook URL to register, and nothing at the point of action checks one against the other. The agent thereby supplies the approval click that a consent screen reserves for the account holder. We measure this failure on two authorization surfaces, an OAuth-style access grant and a webhook registration, with agents built on an open-source browser framework and models from two providers. Without a defense the unauthorized action completed in all 73 attack runs. An instruction telling the model that only the user's task authorizes a grant still left 7 of 10 consent attacks completing. We therefore move the check to where the action completes. The authority envelope gate has the service accept a request only when it matches the task's envelope, the client and account or the webhook URL that the user's task named, fixed before the agent starts. With the gate the agent still sent the request in every one of 70 attack runs, the service rejected each, and the action completed in every control run whose task named it. A service that receives the task's envelope should therefore check agent-driven authorization requests against it.
item.dc:creator: Md Imran Hossen

item.title: On the Effectiveness of NetFlow-Based Deanonymization of Tor Onion Services (Extended Version)
item.description: arXiv:2610.15198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the context of Tor, deanonymization attacks via traffic correlation have long been studied for both clients and onion services. Complementing prior investigations that utilize fine-grained flow metadata such as packet sizes and timings, we study a relatively less explored yet easier-to-obtain adversarial capability: deanonymization using only coarse NetFlow-style telemetry, such as one-minute, 1-out-of-1,000 sampled packet counts. We first revisit active NetFlow-based traffic analysis attacks against Tor onion services and show, through large-scale experiments with live Tor data, that coarse telemetry is sufficient to deanonymize a targeted onion service when the adversary can induce discernible traffic patterns through controlled downloads. We then introduce a stronger active attack based on controlled introduction requests, which removes application-specific assumptions and gives adversaries more flexibility while achieving comparable success rates. Finally, we present a passive deanonymization attack that sends zero traffic to target onion services. The attack exploits Tor's puzzle-based DoS defense as a side channel: public puzzle difficulty reveals service-load changes that can be semantically matched against NetFlow traces. Our findings show that coarse network telemetry poses a practical deanonymization threat to onion services today and call for proactive mitigations and a redesign of the globally visible defense signals that may leak service-load information.
item.dc:creator: Jinseo Lee, Jongkook Han, Yixin Sun, Min Suk Kang

item.title: Asymptotics of Random-Lattice Enumeration: Beyond HKZ via Dense Sublattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.15265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To bridge the gap between worst-case and heuristic analyses of lattice enumeration, we study the sizes of (unpruned) enumeration trees on $n$-dimensional Haar-random lattices. Writing $n^{cn+o(n)}$ for the tree size at the shortest vector radius, we investigate the asymptotic scaling of $c$, and which bases minimize it. For quasi-HKZ bases, we rigorously analyze the random-lattice HKZ geometry and establish $c=1/(2e)\approx 0.1839$. This matches the worst-case enumeration exponent of Hanrot-Stehl\'{e} and confirms earlier predictions for the geometry of HKZ bases on random lattices. Searching beyond quasi-HKZ bases, we prove that with high probability, the minimum achievable tree size exponent $c$ over all bases of a random lattice satisfies: \begin{align} 0.1464 \approx \frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4}\leq c<0.1474. \end{align} For the lower bound, we use Kim's mean-value formula for nested chains of primitive sublattices to rule out bases with small prefix determinants. This strengthens the earlier Rankin-based heuristic lower bound exponent $c \geq 1/8$, discussed by Nguyen and Hanrot-Stehl\'{e}, and rules out the existence of random-lattice bases with trees as small as predicted by the geometric series assumption. For the upper bound, we show that with high probability a dense primitive half-rank sublattice exists with determinant at most $n^{n/8 + o(n)}$. Combining dual HKZ on this sublattice with HKZ on its quotient gives a basis with $c \leq 1/(4\sqrt{e}) \approx 0.1516$. Recursively splitting each half lowers the upper bound below $0.1474$, and under a natural heuristic assumption we prove that the lower bound is tight. Combined with the collision search of Feng-Gao-Liu, our two-block construction gives a polynomial-space algorithm solving the closest vector problem with preprocessing (CVPP) on random lattices in query time $n^{0.0892 n + o(n)}$ for arbitrary targets.
item.dc:creator: Thijs Laarhoven

item.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.15390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
item.dc:creator: Binhong Wang, Haidong Kang, Yanfeng Zhang, Hong-Ning Dai, Guo Yu, Shangce Gao

item.title: Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.15396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.
item.dc:creator: Tianhao Mao, Zihao Wang, Dongfang Zhao, Rui Zhu, Xiaofeng Wang, Haixu Tang

item.title: Security in LLM-Assisted Coding: A Systematic Literature Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.15482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models accelerate software development but introduce severe security vulnerabilities. This systematic review investigates security risks in automated coding, benchmark limitations, and the role of human developers. Findings indicate that models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches due to training data biases. Additionally, the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks. Current evaluation methods suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. Consequently, human oversight remains essential. Safer integration of automation will require more security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and more effective human-AI collaboration frameworks to mitigate these systemic risks.
item.dc:creator: Liang Yuan, Maryam Khanian Najafabadi, Mashud Rana, Varvara Vetrova

item.title: From Observations to Authorized Actions: Measuring Source Information in Android Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.15502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android agents read content from applications and web pages and act on it with the user's authority, yet they cannot reliably tell where that content came from -- its source, the application or document that supplied it. The WebView accessibility fields we inspected expose the host application but omit the document origins available inside the browser, so an agent reading through this interface cannot check which document supplied an object; a limited reproduction on an unmodified WebView yields the same finding. We build and separately evaluate two prototypes to examine how source information supports authorization. Our application-source monitor withholds side-effecting calls whose signed source record contains an untrusted application. With the source set derived from the OS accessibility log, it blocked every selected attack write in the tested runs, but it also withheld benign sends issued after reading untrusted content, flagged benign tasks that use external content, and carried source records into a later clean task. Our WebView source-reference gate uses records from a modified browser to check object origins and reference lifetime through direct calls; in a separate 24-trial evaluation, the live agent selected no disallowed object. Supporting benchmark and planner measurements characterize textual argument matches and attacker-target selection, without establishing causal dataflow or a controlled model ranking. The prototypes are not an integrated defense: the WebView gate still lacks authenticated browser delivery and atomic capture of selected bytes and origin. Together, the results show which source information the tested policies need and why it must stay linked to the object used in execution.
item.dc:creator: Hyobin Ahn, Dongjae Lee

item.title: Poisoned into Action: Context Attacks on Typed Decision Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.15537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision interfaces restrict models to predefined actions, yet schema-valid choices can still trigger policy-violating state changes. Evaluating context poisoning thus requires connecting model decisions to execution outcomes while accounting for legitimate automation retained by defenses. We introduce an execution-aware protocol tracing poisoned evidence through retrieval, model choice, automated action, and persisted state. We evaluate it with 1,659 fresh calls to Jev-1.13.0 across 20 development tasks in two synthetic workflows, using three repetitions per condition. Under natural retrieval, a standalone payload reaches all 60 trials and produces five security-violating executions, while a carrier-payload pair exposes the payload in 57 trials and produces one violation. An initial source-exclusion gate blocks the pair's observed violation but also withholds ten otherwise correct attacked decisions and sixteen correct clean decisions. Correcting its empty-scope behavior restores twelve clean decisions without additional model calls. Factorial controls show that adding correct evidence reduces wrong executions from 119/120 to 55/120 in the semantic arm and from 60/120 to zero in the neutral arm, suggesting that much of the improvement reflects general evidence value rather than attack-specific protection. Three prespecified contrasts are not statistically supported after Holm correction, so the findings remain exploratory. The protocol provides an auditable framework for studying which poisoning-induced errors reach execution and how much correct automation defenses preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/WuXixiong/jev-poisoning-bench.
item.dc:creator: Chenkai Wu, Xing Chang, Jun Yan

item.title: Fetch Me If You Can: A Comprehensive Analysis of Fetch Metadata
item.description: arXiv:2610.15541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective server-side defenses against cross-site attacks depend on understanding the context in which browser requests are generated. However, servers often lack the information needed to distinguish legitimate requests from potentially malicious cross-site interactions. Fetch Metadata, a security mechanism introduced in 2019, addresses this limitation by adding a set of HTTP headers to outgoing browser requests. These headers provide servers with information about a request's context and provenance, enabling them to enforce request isolation policies accordingly. However, the extent of Fetch Metadata's real-world adoption and its interaction with existing security mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first large-scale measurement study of Fetch Metadata adoption. We analyze the top 1M websites in the Tranco list to detect deployments of Fetch Metadata isolation policies and identify custom policies used in the wild. We then examine how these policies address cross-site threats and assess their security coverage. Finally, we provide the first systematic comparison of Fetch Metadata with existing client-side security mechanisms, revealing security gaps that arise from differences between client-side and server-side enforcement.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Bernardo, Alex Ploner, Marco Squarcina, Mauro Tempesta, Matteo Maffei

item.title: Riemannian Suppression of Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG
item.description: arXiv:2610.15626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recorded for motor-imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) carries subject-identifying structure that persists across sessions, allowing separately released sessions from the same person to be linked. Existing EEG identity protections use learned or additive perturbations and operate on representations other than the covariance geometry underlying MI pipelines. We ask whether cross-session identity leakage can be suppressed directly in this covariance representation without learning a privacy model. We introduce a Riemannian transform that equalizes two subject-conditioned geometric statistics: the Riemannian mean covariance and the tangent-space scatter around it, with two optional band-specific refinements. Ablations show that mean alignment and scatter whitening carry nearly all of the suppression, while the optional stages contribute small, dataset-dependent refinements. Across two public datasets and five attackers spanning four covariance-space representations, the worst attacker falls from 90.8% to 15.6% on BCI Competition IV-2a and from 90.8% to 9.9% on OpenBMI, at a cost of 7.0 and 2.1 points of MI decoding accuracy relative to the 8-30 Hz input, and no aggregation rule exceeds chance by more than two points at any batch size. The transform requires no learned privacy model, surrogate network, or gradient-based training, and is fitted on one session and applied unchanged to a held-out later session.
item.dc:creator: Sheikh Samit Muhaimin, Aarthy Nagarajan

item.title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.15725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW-based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open-source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills.
item.dc:creator: Alan Tang, Lifeng Wang, Gang Wu, Tao Zhang, Yantao Jia, Xiaofeng Zhu

item.title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
item.description: arXiv:2610.15729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.
item.dc:creator: Junming Liu, Marcel B\"ohme

item.title: Privacy Conductor: An Architectural Enforcement of Contextual Integrity in LLM-Based Document Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2610.15804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) that retrieve internal documents within an organization must decide who may receive them. Existing approaches based on Contextual Integrity ask the model to make that decision, so access depends on probabilistic reasoning. We present Privacy Conductor, an architecture that removes the decision from the model: a deterministic gate enforces a policy written by an authority, and the model receives only what the requester may already see. On a synthetic clinical corpus of 2,520 requester--document flows, the gate reproduces its policy exactly, so the remaining risk lies in the document labels it reads. As label source is of primary importance, we compare LLM and human generated labels. Across seven configurations of six models from two model families, LLM-written labels degrade the policy in every case. Models assign a document's sensitivity tier correctly on 78--86% of documents, but reproduce its access-control list on as few as 23%. Relabeling the same documents five times with an identical request changes 13 to 124 access decisions per configuration, a result that does not depend on our own labels. On 214 flows from HIPAA court cases, the most accurate configuration (87.8%) still permits 11 of the 20 disclosures the law prohibits. LLMs can describe what a document contains, but not decide who should receive it. Hence, we recommend privacy policy should be authored by accountable personnel and enforced outside the model.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Thornton, Mir Mehedi A. Pritom, Maanak Gupta, Jessee Roberts

item.title: Penetrating the Reality Wall: Long-Range and Through-Wall AR/VR Privacy Eavesdropping via Wireless Power Side Channel
item.description: arXiv:2610.15865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decade, Metaverse technology (AR/VR) has seen widespread adoption in numerous areas, including gaming, social networking, and online collaboration. Although recent studies have exposed vulnerabilities in VR systems, they often apply methods (e.g., pre-installed malicious apps or scripts) from conventional mobile platforms directly, demonstrating impractical attacks that fail to investigate unique privacy leakages specific to VR platforms. In this paper, we present an orthogonal attempt to analyze the attack surface of the power side channel on AR/VR's network connection by capturing the through-wall wireless power in the network transmission medium (e.g., Wi-Fi signals) non-intrusively in a comparatively long distance (e.g., 5.0m-8.0m) and further reconstructing multi-level privacy-aware user behaviors. We propose MetaSpy to validate the feasibility and practicality of our disclosed wireless power-based traffic analysis attack. It first captures through-wall wireless power transmitted from the Wi-Fi router of an adjacent room, identifies the device type, then infers (i) user interactions such as browsing websites, running AR/VR apps, and performing various in-app activities, (ii) unseen VR-specific activities in VR games (e.g., Population: ONE), and (iii) avatar-based user re-identification and virtual keystroke inference corresponding to head movements. We evaluated the effectiveness of MetaSpy in four commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) VR headsets, and the empirical results demonstrate its competitive accuracy in unveiling multi-level user privacy within virtual scenes in through-wall settings at a longer distance (1.8x-80x) than most of the recent studies, and it shows resilience to a series of external interference and impact factors. In addition, we also propose and evaluate effective countermeasures to protect data confidentiality in AR/VR wireless transmission.
item.dc:creator: Tao Ni, Zehua Sun, Yihe Zhou, Yuefeng Du, Qingchuan Zhao, Cong Wang

item.title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.15883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. We first implement it exactly as a serving-time span veto: blocking information flow out of a marked span makes every outside activation bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content, a noninterference property we verify across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B-120B parameters. The veto serves as a deployable quarantine, an exact reference for calibrating leakage, and a teacher. Distilled into weights, it yields a backdoor: checkpoints trained on six model families from 4B to 120B ignore marked context at little benchmark cost, and their outputs show no measurable semantic trace of the suppressed content above the veto reference on our held-out suite; an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review. Detection is therefore a white-box problem. Simpler backdoors remain internally transparent -- linear probes recover suppressed content at 0.57-0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance -- but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention from outside the span into it below the range of base models. Across the attacks we evaluate, probe visibility trades off against routing visibility; we do not establish that this tradeoff is fundamental.
item.dc:creator: Mark Russinovich

item.title: Forensic Text Recovery from Document Thumbnails Using Text-Aware U-Net
item.description: arXiv:2610.15902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forensic analysis of low-resolution Word thumbnails presents a significant challenge because these artifacts may constitute the only remaining visual evidence of deleted documents. Standard Optical Character Recognition (OCR) tools perform poorly on such severely degraded images, creating a critical bottleneck in forensic evidence recovery. Although deep learning architectures, such as U-Net, can improve visual image quality, models optimized solely using pixel-based loss functions tend to favor visual smoothness over the structural fidelity required for accurate text recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a text-aware restoration framework designed for forensic triage. The proposed approach employs a U-Net architecture guided by a hybrid optimization strategy that integrates pixel-level fidelity with machine-readable text constraints. Specifically, an OCR-based Normalized Levenshtein Distance (NLD) metric is used during model selection to prioritize the recovery of an accurate character topology. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the NLD, enabling reliable recovery of machine-readable text from severely degraded thumbnails.

item.dc:creator: Mohit Ajaykumar Dhabuwala, Weifeng Xu

item.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.15924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities. We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Chong Zeng, Ziqian Zhong, Kexun Zhang, Ivan Bercovich, Ivgeni Segal, Yuzhen Mao, Shashwat Saxena, Aditi Raghunathan

item.title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
item.dc:creator: Salma Aboelmagd, Md. Rakibul Ahasan, Zhixin Pan, Abdulrahman Takiddin, Ziyu Shu

item.title: CreepScope: Measuring Post-Use Authorization Exposure in Tool-Using Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.15988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. We study this lifecycle failure as privilege creep: a capability stays reachable after its last justified workflow step. We present CreepScope, a trace-oriented evaluation protocol that samples reachable authority at every step and separates no-remaining-use exposure into stale-after-use and never-required components; Capability-Step Exposure (CSE) counts total stepwise overexposure and Residual Privilege Debt (RPD) the terminal residue, while stale-after-use exposure is the direct privilege-creep measure. A 96-cell deterministic replay over 12 controlled storage, communication, and cloud-operation workflows validates these semantics: Static Task Scope and Monotonic On-Demand retain mean CSEs of 26 and 13, whereas an oracle-controlled Step Lease has zero CSE and zero residual debt by construction. All three persistent regimes share the same stale-after-use exposure of 13, so their CSE differences come from scope and grant timing rather than post-use retention; Full Access alone adds 91.33 never-required capability-steps. A separate 24-episode local case then lets Qwen2 7B choose tools in one simulated mail workflow: the injected stale send executes in all nine persistent-policy episodes and in none of the three Step-Lease episodes, while all 24 required action sequences complete. These results establish a reproducible containment case, not cross-workflow or cross-model effectiveness. Core metrics are reconstructed from raw events, and exact gates reject incomplete or duplicated evaluation grids.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu, Danping Zhang, Su Wang, Pin Qian, Yihang Chen, Xiaochong Jiang

item.title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
item.description: arXiv:2610.15995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal.
