The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.
item.dc:creator: Anoop Mishra, Joshua Moore, Aly Sabri Abdalla, Vuk Marojevic

item.title: DelegateGuard: Purpose-Bound Capabilities for Delegated LLM Agent Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.16005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: \textbf{(Context)} LLM agents increasingly delegate subtasks while holding authority over sensitive data, creating confused-deputy risks: an injected delegate can exfiltrate data, amplify its authority, or act after revocation. Existing leakage benchmarks expose these failures but do not constrain the authority a delegated agent may exercise. \textbf{(Methods)} We present \system, a reference monitor that converts the initiating user's authorization into attenuable capabilities over purpose, labels, operations, sinks, and delegation depth; every data-moving action is mediated outside the LLM, and revocation cascades through the delegation graph. We formalize a trace-level safety invariant and evaluate it with an adaptive within-authority adversary and four baselines, model-action and multi-turn ecological studies, and conformance and scale checks over deterministic traces and 517{,}401 Enron emails. \textbf{(Results)} \system blocks ungranted-sink exfiltration, authority amplification, revocation replay, purpose gaming, and intra-tool label violations, and dominates static allowlists on the revocation and intra-tool cases (10/10). Two open models proposed attacker-goal actions on 42/45 and 44/45 injected traces, all blocked at execution; a 90-run multi-turn study cut leakage from 0.844 to 0.20 with full task completion, at microsecond per-decision overhead. Proposition~1 characterizes exactly where attenuation-based authorization suffices, a boundary we also reproduce empirically across four observable-sink workflows. \textbf{(Conclusion \& Significance)} Purpose-bound runtime authorization gives delegated LLM workflows a model-independent execution boundary and a precise recipe for composing it with declassification and content monitoring on externally observable sinks.
item.dc:creator: Phat T. Tran-Truong, Ha Vo, Nhut Tran, Khang Vo, Thai-Minh Truong

item.title: Adversarial Robustness of Camera-Radar Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Driving
item.description: arXiv:2610.16012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous driving (AD) relies on multi-sensor perception to interpret the surrounding environment. However, the robustness of camera--radar fusion under adversarial conditions remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic measurement study of the robustness of camera--radar sensor fusion in AD. We construct a unified evaluation pipeline on the nuScenes dataset that simulates attacks on both sensing modalities, including eight camera-image perturbations and three radar point-cloud perturbations. We evaluate five camera--radar fusion algorithms across two perception tasks, 3D object detection and depth estimation, and quantify their performance under clean and attacked inputs using standard metrics. Our evaluation reveals a clear asymmetry in the robustness of fusion systems. Camera perturbations substantially degrade both object detection and depth estimation, and moderate attack strengths are already sufficient to cause severe performance degradation. In contrast, the evaluated radar perturbations produce smaller and task-dependent effects, with object-detection models showing particularly limited degradation. Our analysis attributes this difference to the strong dependence of existing fusion architectures on dense camera features, together with the filtering, association, and confidence-weighting mechanisms commonly applied to sparse radar measurements. These results demonstrate that sensor fusion does not inherently guarantee robustness and that the contribution and reliability of each sensing modality must be explicitly considered under adversarial conditions. Based on four empirical findings, we derive measurement-guided design implications for future robust camera--radar fusion, including modality-specific reliability estimation, cross-modal consistency checking, adaptive fusion, and graceful failover under severe sensor degradation.
item.dc:creator: Ce Zhou, Yubo Wu, Khang Nguyen, Liyang Xiao, Thomas Hou, Qiben Yan

item.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.
item.dc:creator: Sunday Oyinlola Ogundoyin, Muhammad Ikram

item.title: Confidential Error-Correcting Codes
item.description: arXiv:2610.16087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. We formalize this primitive through three security properties: confidentiality, robustness, and soundness. To realize this goal, we develop a general framework for constructing CECs based on a Randomness-Security Separation (RSS) structure, which first encodes a nonce to introduce randomness and then masks the encoded payload with a pseudorandom function. Based on our RSS framework, we instantiate CECs, called Conc-CEC, using concatenated Reed-Muller and Reed-Solomon codes. The resulting Conc-CEC admits provable guarantees for all three properties. Notably, compared to PRCs (CRYPTO'24), another recent cryptographic primitive with error-correcting capability, CECs achieve significantly stronger concrete security guarantees under practical parameter settings. As a primary application of CECs, we further present CECMark, a watermarking scheme for AI-generated images. Our experiments on real-world generative image models show that CECMark consistently outperforms state-of-the-art watermarking methods, including Gaussian Shading (CVPR'24), PRCMark (ICLR'25), and T2SMark (NeurIPS'25). In particular, CECMark achieves higher robustness across all 56 evaluated perturbations and ensures a false positive rate below $10^{-5}$ without introducing side effects. Taken together, our work lays a novel cryptographic foundation for trustworthy watermarking schemes that, for the first time, unify provable security guarantees with strong practical reliability.
item.dc:creator: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Delong Ran, Xiaoyun Wang

item.title: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
item.description: arXiv:2610.16100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes a shared key without leaving transferable evidence that a party participated. We study DAKE protocols that authenticate each fresh session with one ring signature and show that their deniability mechanisms fall into three authentication allocations: sharing an authentication witness, hiding the signing witness under a fixed ring, or varying the verified ring between real and simulated executions. For fixed-ring protocols, witness hiding yields a necessary relation between the ring signature's witness-indistinguishability gap and the protocol's $(\mu,\delta)$ deniability parameters. We instantiate witness hiding in HDKEM, a three-slot hybrid that combines ML-KEM-768, X25519, and an optional pairwise information-theoretic source through a split-key PRF. HDKEM binds all public session values, including a QKD key identifier when present, into authentication and key derivation. Under the stated component models, it achieves eCK key indistinguishability, forward secrecy, and strong local deniability. We evaluate HDKEM with FalconRS and Gandalf. Across 2,000 primitive operations, median signing/verification times are 9.20/1.02 ms for FalconRS and 18.61/0.97 ms for Gandalf in our reference environment. In source-backed mode, the corresponding TCP-application costs are 8,607 B and 8,555 B per handshake. A separate 500-session server experiment exercises the complete FalconRS source-backed path and reports a median server time of 16.29 ms including local I/O.
item.dc:creator: Kazi Hassan Shakib, Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, Arslan Munir

item.title: ML-Assisted Power Side-Channel Attacks on ML Accelerators in Shared FPGAs
item.description: arXiv:2610.16164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud providers offer on-demand access to Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and multi-tenant FPGAs let multiple users share one device to improve utilization. This sharing introduces security risks: an adversary co-located with a victim on the same FPGA can mount power side-channel attacks against the victim's Machine Learning (ML) accelerator. Prior on-chip attacks on such accelerators based on Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) sensors have recovered only small, MNIST-scale grayscale inputs, including with ML-assisted reconstruction. This work is the first on-chip, TDC-based attack to produce full-scale color reconstructions of ImageNet-scale inputs, by combining ML-based upscaling and recoloring with TDC measurements of a remote victim's ML accelerator. We frame this as a proof-of-concept leakage study: the victim implements the first convolution layer of a CNN processing 224x224 ImageNet inputs on a shared FPGA, which we isolate to characterize the input-dependent leakage, and we quantify how much of each reconstruction reflects genuinely recovered information versus ML-generated post-processing. As a preliminary countermeasure, we study a pixel-substitution defense that replaces each pixel value, within a fixed intensity budget, with one of different Hamming Weight, producing a different TDC signature. We find that this transformation costs the victim's own model more accuracy than it costs the attacker and, because it applies the same fixed, publicly reconstructable mapping to every image, is largely defeated by an attacker retrained on the transformed data; robust defenses will require randomized or input-dependent transformations.
item.dc:creator: Anthony Etim, Kenan Erol, Jakub Szefer

item.title: ATTCK-R: Knowledge-Aware Long-Horizon Jailbreaking for Protected LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.16305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models are deployed behind increasingly sophisticated safety mechanisms, evaluating their robustness under realistic adversarial conditions becomes increasingly difficult and critical. Existing jailbreaking evaluations often rely on static prompts, limited interaction horizons, or lightly protected systems, failing to reflect protected deployment settings with prompt-based safety protections. We show that the introduction of a prompt-based safety protection reduces the average attack success rate of a strong multi-turn baseline from 0.896 to 0.608 (32.1\% relative), demonstrating that unprotected evaluations substantially overestimate real-world vulnerabilities. We propose Adaptive Traceback and Tactic Curation for Knowledge-based Red-teaming (ATTCK-R), a planning-driven multi-turn red teaming framework designed for protected black-box systems. ATTCK-R models jailbreaking as a long-horizon trajectory optimization problem using a structured belief state, introduces optimization-based tactic curation to abstract reusable strategies from prior successes and failures, and employs informed traceback to resume attacks from strategically meaningful states rather than restarting. Evaluated across 9 widely used LLMs configured with a single prompt-based safety protection layer, ATTCK-R consistently outperforms strong recent multi-turn jailbreaking frameworks. Ablation results confirm that long-horizon planning and tactic curation improve attack effectiveness, while adaptive traceback improves efficiency through structured recovery from conversational failure.
item.dc:creator: Md Mushfiqur Rahman, Tobias Rohde, Rahul Tripathi, Khalil Elkhalil, Kevin Lybarger

item.title: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.16336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher-enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher-held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier-phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release-specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key-preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance metadata with release-specific face verification and record-linked evidence for further assessment.
item.dc:creator: Chia-Ming Lee, Chia-Yu Lin, Hung-Kai Huang, Yi-Ting Ku, Yu-Chen Liang, Chih-Chung Hsu

item.title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
item.description: arXiv:2610.16373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Shakiba, Hamid Reza Ghaeini, Sadegh Dorri Nogoorani

item.title: Risk-aware Road-network Trajectory Synthesis under Local Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2610.16384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Road-network trajectory synthesis under local differential privacy (LDP) enables mobility data analysis without uploading raw trajectories to an untrusted server. Existing locally private trajectory synthesis methods mainly model whole trajectories, point sequences, or grid-level mobility patterns. However, they cannot handle non-uniform privacy risks caused by local road-network and trajectory contexts, such as endpoints, long-stay-associated regions, and low-out-degree branches. They also do not directly protect conditional next-hop choices on road networks, where a user's selected successor may reveal sensitive local movement intentions. To address these challenges, we propose TrajRACE, a locally private synthesis framework for road-network trajectories. TrajRACE uses start, segment-count, and transition reports to represent trajectories. For each transition, it keeps the current road segment as a public aggregation context and perturbs the true successor among legal successors on the client side. It then assigns risk-aware protection strengths to transitions according to local road-network and trajectory contexts. Finally, the server recovers population-level start, segment-count, and conditional transition statistics from heterogeneous privatized reports, and generates synthetic trajectories that follow the public road-network topology. Experiments on three road-network trajectory datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TrajRACE in improving synthetic-data utility across distributional, query-based, and pattern-level metrics, while providing stronger protection for high-risk local transitions.
item.dc:creator: Hongzhen Xiang, Chenxu Wang, Yumeng Song, Tao Qin, Yushuai Li, Pinghui Wang, Wei Wang

item.title: Purpose IR: Compiling User Purpose for Privacy-Preserving Agent Workflow State
item.description: arXiv:2610.16414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest high-privacy baseline by 27.5 PCS points. On 493 PrivacyLens trajectories, it achieves the highest Safe Action Rate at 77.3%, 10.4 points above the next-best method, extending the same boundary from reusable state to downstream actions. These results show that privacy-preserving agent state requires more than filtering sensitive or task-irrelevant content: it requires an explicit, executable representation of what the user's purpose authorizes to survive.
item.dc:creator: Dongsheng Chen, Xiangyu Zhao, Lei Ma, Xin Yao, Xuetao Wei

item.title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
item.description: arXiv:2610.16449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.
item.dc:creator: Runang He, Tongya Zheng, Jing Cao, Yucheng Ying, Shunyu Liu, Bingde Hu, Yang Gao, Zeyuan Hu, Jianrong Zhang, Mingli Song

item.title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.16458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Xiuyuan Qi, Yi Wang, Wenjie Wang

item.title: CircuitBreak: Pruning a Sparse Safety Circuit of Neurons
item.description: arXiv:2610.16470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: White-box neuron pruning has shown that refusal in large language models (LLMs) can depend on a small, removable set of feed-forward (FFN) channels. Existing attacks either need carefully paired ``twin'' prompts or score each neuron in isolation. Pruning also has an unavoidable capability cost, so over-removal compounds the loss. TwinBreak removes $1\%$--$5\%$ of parameters and NeuroStrike removes $0.3\%$--$0.7\%$ of neurons in targeted layers. We model safety as a small \emph{circuit} whose neurons contribute jointly rather than independently. We propose \textsc{CircuitBreak}, a neuron-pruning attack that greedily searches for a sparse set of FFN neurons whose joint ablation flips a refusal readout. \textsc{CircuitBreak} re-scores every candidate after the neurons already removed and needs no twin prompts. On ten instruction-tuned models, the greedy search converges after removing $29$--$150$ neurons ($0.0066\%$--$0.0388\%$ of the MLP). The pruned models raise the attack success rate from $2.24\%$/$7.35\%$ to $87.54\%$/$87.54\%$ on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from $8.95\%$/$5.43\%$ to $88.50\%$/$88.18\%$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, as judged by Llama Guard 3 8B on StrongREJECT.
item.dc:creator: Jincheng Ying, Li Wenlin, Wencheng Yang, Yinhao Xiao

item.title: CT0: Cybersecurity Transformer
item.description: arXiv:2610.16550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for the facts it is unsure about, extracts vulnerability facts more accurately than either mode alone at a fifth of the generative cost. All of it is built in about 314 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours and served from one workstation GPU, with no policy layer between operator and target. Across eighteen benchmarks and use cases run with one checkpoint and head, we report where the design helps, where it does not, and what it still lacks.
item.dc:creator: V\'ictor Mayoral-Vilches

item.title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.16778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.
item.dc:creator: Zian Yuan, Wei Li

item.title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
item.description: arXiv:2610.16790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.
item.dc:creator: Shaomin Chen, Xiaorui Gong

item.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
item.description: arXiv:2610.16814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.
item.dc:creator: Anning Hu, Yangyu Li, Yuqi Huang, Shengchao Hu, Junchi Yan

item.title: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
item.dc:creator: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn

item.title: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.
item.dc:creator: Assunta Imperatrice, Luigi ROmano

item.title: Security and robustness analysis of encrypted communications for local home automation: ESPHome Native API and MQTT over TLS 1.3
item.description: arXiv:2610.16928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in residential and local automation environments has highlighted the limitations of considering the internal network as an inherently trusted domain. Man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, such as ARP spoofing, can allow traffic interception or manipulation when communications lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, and authentication mechanisms. This paper presents a systematized review of the security mechanisms used by two communication alternatives between ESP-family microcontrollers and the Home Assistant platform: MQTT protected through TLS 1.3 and the ESPHome Native API, whose encryption is based on the Noise Protocol Framework using the Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 pattern. The analysis considers four dimensions: cryptographic robustness, attack surface, implementation complexity, and resource consumption. The review identifies significant differences resulting from the architecture and cryptographic model of each alternative. TLS 1.3 provides a standardized framework compatible with public-key infrastructure and formal identity management, though it introduces greater configuration complexity and computational overhead during session establishment. The ESPHome Native API employs a more specialized scheme with lower operational complexity, eliminates dynamic algorithm negotiation, and uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. The resource-consumption analysis relies on measurements published by the projects and manufacturers themselves, not on an experimental test bench, and this limitation is explicitly acknowledged. The results identify the conditions under which each mechanism is appropriate for local home-automation architectures and provide a basis for designing IoT systems that balance security, interoperability, and resource constraints.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: International Journal of Network Security & Its Applications (IJNSA), vol. 18, no. 4/5, 2026, pp. 15-35
item.dc:creator: Carlos Roberto Gonzalez-Escarpeta, Juan Eduardo Garcia Sanchez, Jos\'e Antonio Hernandez Reyes, Ricardo Francisco Martinez-Gonzalez

item.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
item.description: arXiv:2610.17020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega, Ajay Jagannath, Adit Jain, Guram Gogia, Soumyadeep Bakshi, Nazneen Rajani

item.title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.
item.dc:creator: Mingfei Yu, Chenglu Jin, Giovanni De Micheli

item.title: SEAL-DT: An End-to-End Security Engineering and Assurance Framework for Cross-Domain Digital Twins
item.description: arXiv:2610.17097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber-physical systems connect physical processes, software, networks and organizations. Securing them requires a clear account of what happened, what was observed, which actions were authorized and what evidence supports each decision. Digital Twin (DT) descriptions often fail to explain how these elements stay consistent, blur the distinction between physical events and uncertain observations, or detach simulation results from their requirements and assumptions. This paper presents SEAL-DT (Security Engineering and Assurance Lifecycle for Digital Twins), a structured approach to building and evaluating secure DTs. It brings entity definitions, process models, deterministic simulations, data contracts, evidence records, automated tests and reproducible results into one connected model. The main contribution is an end-to-end DT security framework, spanning scenario definition, entity/process modelling, simulation, security decision logic, evidence handling, validation and reproducible reporting. Security decisions and simulation results thus trace back to their data, assumptions and requirements. A DT is more than a copy of system state: it states what it can observe, how accurate and current its information is, where it came from and which decisions it may support. We demonstrate SEAL-DT in five scenarios: Car2X protection, passive IoT-device detection, an industrial control surrogate, lawful acquisition in a smart home, and medical-IoT monitoring that preserves continuity of care. Each includes formal models, deterministic and negative experiments, uncertainty analyses, schema-valid fixtures, technical reports and verified manifests, testing multiple configurations under normal and adverse conditions. Results show that the framework supports consistent model construction, traceable execution and comparable internal validation, and that security findings link to observable evidence.
item.dc:creator: Iraklis Varlamis, Stelios Zindros, Christos Sardianos, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos

item.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.17126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.
item.dc:creator: Ahammod Munim Ramil, Khalid Al Kafi, M. A. Abdullahis Sany, Muktadirul Islam Nibir, Md Yeasin Ali, Mohammad Zavid Parvez, Md Sadek Ferdous

item.title: Tight End-to-End Accounting for Differentially Private Synthetic Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.17249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentially private (DP) pipelines often combine heterogeneous mechanisms, yet their guarantees are best analyzed using different notions of privacy (e.g., bounded range, zCDP, ADP). When composing them, we have to analyze the guarantees through a reduced common representation that loses accounting precision. This issue is particularly relevant in DP synthetic data generation, where data preprocessing, generation algorithms, and DP-SGD could appear within the same pipeline. We develop novel tools for tight end-to-end accounting of such compositions using privacy loss distributions (PLD), $f$-DP, and Gaussian DP (GDP). In particular, we derive PLD and GDP analyses of bounded-range mechanisms such as the Exponential mechanism. Building on these theoretical results, we introduce AIM-GDP, a GDP-native variant of AIM (a state-of-the-art DP synthetic data mechanism) that enables easy composability with complex pipelines via PLD, attack-aware risk calibration, and tight end-to-end auditing while consistently achieving better utility; and MixCal, an algorithm for calibrating adaptive mixed compositions using PLD accounting. Overall, our tools enable tighter end-to-end accounting and thus less noise at the same privacy level in DP synthetic data pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Georgi Ganev, Vadym Doroshenko, Arun Ganesh, Juan Felipe Gomez, Ryan McKenna, Bogdan Kulynych

item.title: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
item.description: arXiv:2610.17313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned LLMs show that TRAP outperforms its counterparts on six models under the reported method settings and the common primary evaluator, achieving attack success rates of 45.6% to 97.9% on these models. These findings support hierarchical strategy learning as an effective approach to discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Reza Mirbagheri, Amir Mahdi Sadeghzadeh

item.title: VeriRouter: Towards Verifiable LLM Routing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers are increasingly deployed to optimize quality, latency, and cost through dynamic model selection and request rewriting. However, a compromised router can cause ineligible selection on the control plane, unendorsed rewriting or unfaithful relay on the data plane, undermining LLM routing integrity. We present VeriRouter, a verifiable LLM routing framework. Under an endorsed public context binding a private semantic index and rewrite banks, VeriRouter combines ZK proofs with a provider-issued serving certificate to establish integrity across both planes while keeping the router's private routing assets hidden from clients. For model selection, we design an efficient ZK proof for semantic search. For rewriting, local checks enforce message preservation and additions from committed banks. On real-world workloads, VeriRouter's model-selection and rewrite proofs average 21.92~s and 4.24~s, yielding 1,307$\times$ and 101$\times$ speedups over the fastest completing baselines. Relative to serving without verification, VeriRouter adds only 4.08 s under per-turn selection and 0.11 s under session-pinned selection.
item.dc:creator: Mengyu Yao, Ziqi Zhang, Shaofei Li, Yifeng Cai, Ding Li, Yao Guo, Ning Luo

item.title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
item.description: arXiv:2610.17457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.
item.dc:creator: Yuetian Chen, Kaiyuan Zhang, Yuntao Du, Thomas Li, Mark Tenenholtz, Kyle Polley, Jerry Ma, Denis Yarats, Ninghui Li

item.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.17523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
item.dc:creator: Maria-Ioana-Andrea Ivan, Orhan Ermis, Ruxandra F. Olimid

item.title: Discovery or Memorization? A Faithful Benchmark for Real-World Business-Logic Vulnerability Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.17542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of cybersecurity agents in vulnerability discovery has increased the need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities accurately. However, synthetic benchmarks lack realism, real-life benchmarks are prone to contamination, and many existing benchmarks have already been saturated by current models. We therefore set out to develop a benchmark that is realistic, reproducible, resistant to contamination, and challenging. Our key insight is that real-life business-logic vulnerabilities are subtle and exercise complex application interactions, making them naturally demanding. The difficulty lies in specifying evaluation criteria precise enough to faithfully measure model capabilities while keeping the tasks free of data-leakage. We introduce AnonVul, a cross-language benchmark of 132 application-level business-logic vulnerabilities, built by a semi-automated pipeline that anonymizes each task, injects oracles from expert-written specifications, and differentially verifies proof-of-concept exploits. The benchmark spans nine languages, with two evaluation tracks on black-box and grey-box settings, where each task runs in a sandbox with specialized oracles embedded in key exploitation steps. We evaluate six state-of-the-art vulnerability-discovery agents on the AnonVul benchmark, measuring discovery success, cost-effectiveness, anonymization sensitivity, oracle validity, and failure modes. Our results show that AnonVul remains challenging, with the best agent succeeding in only 23.11% of attempts. On a matched cohort of 20 vulnerabilities, restoring software identity increases discovery from 21.25% to 40.83%, highlighting the importance of controlling recognizable software knowledge when evaluating vulnerability discovery.
item.dc:creator: Rui Yang, Yichao Xu, Zhuohao Zhang, Jiahao Ji, Chaowei Xiao, Yinzhi Cao, Ziyang Li

item.title: Extending Layered Attestation into ARM Application Run-Times
item.description: arXiv:2610.17614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern mobile and edge platforms provide hardware-backed attestation of application and platform integrity at load-time. However, they offer little support once application execution begins. We present ARA, an Application-Runtime Anchor for ARM that extends this load-time chain of trust into execution. ARA bootstraps from the underlying ARM platform Root of Trust (RoT) through a measured loading chain and establishes an attested protected run-time within the application address space using recently introduced ARM Permission Overlay Extensions (POE). The resulting run-time domain can host programmable RoTs for Measurement and Storage (RTM/RTS), enabling application run-time integrity verification, attestation evidence generation, and protected use of secrets while retaining efficient access to application run-time state. As exemplary uses, we instantiate ARA for protected media decryption and application control flow measurement. Our prototype and evaluation show that ARA supports frequent run-time RoT-backed operations at near in-process cost, with roughly 10x and 50x lower overhead than out-of-process equivalents. This offers a practical bridge from layered attestation to application run-time trusted computing on ARM.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Joia Neto, Bilel Sefsaf, Norrathep Rattanavipanon, Carlos Chinea Perez, Hans Liljestrand, J-Erik Ekberg

item.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
item.description: arXiv:2610.17711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$. (2) For every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+\delta)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\frac{\delta}{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $\delta$. (3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $\eta_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $\eta_c>0$. All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.
item.dc:creator: Hai H. Nguyen

item.title: Beyond Model Scaling: Rethinking Sequence Construction for Transformer-based Network Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.17725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) have shown strong potential for detecting multi-stage cyberattacks, yet most methods construct input sequences using fixed temporalization schemes rather than treating sequence construction as a systems design decision. In flow-based intrusion detection, timestamp-based windowing often fragments related attack activities while merging unrelated communications, reducing the behavioral context available to transformers. We present a unified pipeline abstraction that decomposes transformer-based NIDS into four design dimensions (traffic representation, temporalization, transformer backbone, and prediction aggregation) and propose session-coherent temporalization, which constructs sequences from communication sessions instead of fixed time windows. Experiments on three complementary intrusion detection datasets show that temporalization is the dominant factor governing transformer performance: session-coherent temporalization more than doubles Macro-F1 over timestamp-based windowing, enabling lightweight transformers to achieve up to 0.95 Macro-F1 at substantially higher inference throughput than pretrained models. We further vary the transformer size from 0.65M to 3.38M parameters and find that larger transformer models provide no measurable accuracy improvement despite substantially higher computational cost, while zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation shows only modest gains under domain shift. These results indicate that preserving communication-session semantics, rather than scaling transformer capacity, is the key to accurate and efficient transformer-based intrusion detection.
item.dc:creator: Zeeshan Zulkifl Shah, Muhammad Ikram, Dali Kaafar, Yipeng Zhou

item.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.17727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL.md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
item.dc:creator: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge

item.title: Same Attack, Different Judge: A First Controlled Adversarial Comparison of Jev, LLM Judges, and Purpose-Built Safety Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2610.17820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TypeSafe AI's Jev is a new kind of safety judge. It generates no text and no label: it answers questions the developer defines in advance and returns a probability for each answer. The vendor admits that adversarial input can change these answers but gives no numbers. In this paper, we present the first controlled adversarial evaluation of Jev. We build a test harness that sends every system the same payload under the same policy, and run it on four public-data tasks, from rule-based ones (input moderation, injection detection, routing) to a judgment-based one (phishing detection), with fifty attack variants from thirteen families. The targets are Jev, five GPT and GLM judges, and two local classifiers (Llama Guard 3, Prompt Guard 2). We find that Jev is the most robust system on input moderation: eight forgeries of its structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks, against 56% for GPT-6 Astra. On phishing detection. However, the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags, and even without attack Jev detects only 62% of phishing emails, against 77-81% for the GLM judges. Jev is also the fastest judge, but it flags the most benign requests (27%). The local classifiers fail differently: a training-example statement makes Llama Guard 3 miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged. These results suggest that Jev resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for an overall judgment.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Li, Aichun Huang, Mingming Zhang, Zheli Liu

item.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
item.description: arXiv:2610.17837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
item.dc:creator: Fasheng Miao, Zhaoyu Hu, Xiang Li, Changqing An, Jiutian Zeng, Longtao Huang, Haixin Duan, Jilong Wang

item.title: Provenance and Authorization in Autobiographical Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.17935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autobiographical language models may draw on archives containing observations, quotations, emotional reports, and earlier model outputs. Cryptographic authentication can preserve an archive while leaving these sources semantically conflated. We formulate this gap as a computer-security problem: narrative content must not silently become consent or alter an authorized decision rule. We define typed records, authenticated attestations, a separate policy channel, and admissible views. Under explicit assumptions, we give a standard integrity reduction and a noninterference argument, characterize the information required by exact decision-preserving summaries, and show why passive history and fixed-point convergence need not identify a preferred action. Alpay Algebra supplies a comparative language for iterative memory without being a premise of the proofs. Sociology of religious affiliation, source-monitoring psychology, and self-determination theory motivate distinctions in a bounded Latter-day Saint vignette. A separate, reproducible pilot uses a frozen public language model on 32 wholly synthetic cases across 576 paired conditions. It compares flattened records, source labels, and an explicit admission gate under contradictory summary repetition. The study concerns computational attribution and authorization, not the motives or psychology of the people in the vignette.
item.dc:creator: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay

item.title: Standing, Not Truth: Who May Say What About Whom in Agentic Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.17952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software agents increasingly choose on a user's behalf among competing offerings described by the parties who benefit. A lawful participant, publishing under its own identity, compromising no channel and issuing no instruction, can move that choice with a single false factual claim about a competing offering. Across twelve published defenses spanning the three placements a check can occupy, none separates it from marketing. Each accepts it for a reason correct on its own: its origin is a lawful channel, its influence is evidence meant to decide, its action serves the user's goal. None establishes that the publisher was entitled to speak about a competitor, each exclusion stated by the defenses' own authors. Disclosure does not replace enforcement: re-rendering every description as attributed speech leaves the attack at 72/72, the agent repeating the attribution and reasoning from it. The missing relation is standing: whether a claimant's bound identity entitles it to assert about a claim's subject. A publisher may say what its own package does. It has no standing to say a competitor's package is frozen, and the difference is decidable without settling whether either is true. Deciding it needs the one fact prose extraction does not recover, who spoke, which a catalogue binds to every entry and then drops. The check is quiet on honest traffic, flagging 0.9% of natural pairs in two corpora. Used as a gate it stops 130 of 131 landed attacks and disturbs none of 348 honest selections. Applied everywhere it changes 0.9% and 2.6%, where deleting the whole description changes 12.7% and 21.0%. On thirteen further agents the attack succeeds on 50.7% of decisions and sentence removal leaves 10.3% standing. Two published attacks stay outside: self-directed claims, which standing admits, and injected criteria, with no subject in the set.
item.dc:creator: Yedidel Louck, Amit Dvir, Ariel Stulman

item.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
item.description: arXiv:2610.18007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.
item.dc:creator: Qikun Cai, Tao Huang, Chen Hou

item.title: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
item.description: arXiv:2610.18054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to \textbf{1.65} seconds when optimized for throughput.
item.dc:creator: H. \c{C}a\u{g}r{\i} Bilgi, Kemal Mutluergil, Ceren Y{\i}ld{\i}r{\i}m, Kubilay Atasu, Erkay Savas

item.title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
item.description: arXiv:2610.18230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 42.2% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 83.0% of traces. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Hua, Taro Tsuchiya, Nicolas Christin, Giulia Fanti

item.title: Encrypted Skills Can Become New Security Exploits If AI Agents Know How to Decipher
item.description: arXiv:2610.18262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Third-party skills can expose LLM agents to malicious instructions hidden by encoding. We introduce Ciphered Skill Injection (CSI), which embeds such instructions in skill files for agents to decode and follow. We evaluate Caesar and layered variants across eight models and 139 injection-task pairs, separating instruction recovery from attack success. In the primary setting with shortened skills, the variants achieve attack success rates of up to 47.5% and 40.3%, respectively. Successful decoding does not guarantee attack success, and layering has model-dependent effects. The tested skill scanners rarely flag injected skills. These findings highlight the risk of promoting decoded, untrusted content into actionable instructions.
item.dc:creator: Yan-Lun Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Chia-Mu Yu

item.title: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
item.description: arXiv:2610.18311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a factor of 2.5 and removes that remaining violation. The gain costs a small and deliberate concession in raw deterrence. Twin inference meets the 50 ms budget on a workstation core and an embedded GPU, and is projected to meet it on both edge CPUs when the three envelope stages are evaluated in a single batched call; the complete decision-to-enforcement path was measured only on the workstation.
item.dc:creator: Oscar Mogollon-Gutierrez, Mohammadhossein Homaei, Alberto Lopez-Trigo, Andres Caro, Mar Avila

item.title: Jev-Guard: Fast Routing and Auditing Agent Actions over Editable Policy Trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.18326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses require a low-latency guardrail model together with customizable audit policies. However, deploying an auto-regressive guardrail model remains challenging: such models incur high inference latency and are often poorly aligned with customized policies. To address these problems, we present Jev-Guard, a unified model for safety classification and policy routing. We further construct a policy tree over which Jev-Guard performs routing, spanning diverse domains including content moderation, cybersecurity, privacy, and legal compliance. Specifically, Jev-Guard first navigates the policy tree to select the applicable audit policy given the caller's audit context, and then performs safety classification conditioned on the retrieved policies. On 7,033 evaluation cases, Jev-Guard achieves 93.72\% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms, and 93.10\% hierarchical routing accuracy. The full routing-and-classification pipeline averages 240ms. Furthermore, we integrate Jev-Guard into the Hermes harness framework. Across agent trajectories, its separate permission gate cuts mean review time per task from 4.80s for an SFT-LLM judge to 1.33s, with no policy violations are observed for either guard.
item.dc:creator: Wenbin Hu, Huihao Jing, Haochen Shi, Yuxuan Liu, Changxuan Fan, Sirui Zhang, Kawai Chung, Hanyu Yang, Zhenhuan Wang, Ziyi Chen, Haoran Li, Yangqiu Song

item.title: Pin It on Anyone: Certified Targeted Displacement of Multi-Bit LLM Watermarks Without the Key
item.description: arXiv:2610.18359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-bit watermarking embeds a message, typically an account identifier, into LLM output so that harmful text can be traced to its origin. We show an attack technique that allows to alter the watermarking message. This allows to, for example, exchange the embedded account ID to an arbitrary different one. The attacker mainly needs access to a few accounts for generating LLM output and model logits, but crucially not the secret key used to watermark. The attacker then rewrites the text, keeping its meaning, so that the watermarking message decoder recovers the watermarking message embedded by the attacker. We are, to our knowledge, the first to propose such an attack, which we call a targeted displacement. Theoretically, we present upper and lower bounds on the probability of our attack succeeding.
